APP governance is the missing foundation

JUMP TO

  • Governance is the missing foundation
  • 6 things leading organizations do differently
  • Governance is the missing foundation
  • 6 things leading organizations do differently

SHARE

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 5:26
Instaread

By Milissa Eagle, MA, Director of Workforce Analytics, and Anita Opdycke, DNP, RN, APRN, PMHNP-BC, NP-C, SVP/Partner, Advisory and Consulting

In our previous blog, we explored the advanced practice provider (APP) practice environment, from staffing pressures and resilience challenges to the operational barriers that affect day-to-day work. While those issues are often addressed individually, the organizations making the most progress have realized they share a common thread: how APPs are integrated into organizational leadership and decision-making.

Many workforce challenges that seem operational on the surface may, in fact, be structural. Staffing models, workflows, career development, and professional voice are all shaped by the systems that govern how APPs work.

Governance is the missing foundation

Beneath many of the challenges APPs describe lies a more fundamental issue: role clarity. Role clarity is what governance produces when it works. Its absence is usually the first visible symptom of a governance gap.

Most health systems were designed around physician and nursing leadership structures, while APPs were integrated over time. The outcome is a workforce spread across departments, service lines, and reporting structures without consistent governance or clearly defined expectations.

That creates more operational problems: variability in scope of practice, inconsistent use of the role, fragmented professional identity, and limited participation in governance and shared decision-making. These constrain APPs’ ability to build social capital and professional ownership. Why does that matter so much? Because social capital—i.e., the trust and reciprocity that lets colleagues act on each other’s behalf without renegotiating every interaction—is what turns a credentialed workforce into a high-functioning team.

For APPs, role clarity covers more ground than a job description—for example, how the role contributes to organizational goals, how success gets measured, what professional development looks like, and where they fit within the broader care team.

Our data reinforces just how important that foundation is. APPs rated three items among the lowest-performing measures:

  1. Having adequate input into decisions affecting their practice
  2. Responsiveness to provider feedback
  3. Alignment between provider priorities and leadership actions

These findings are echoed in the feedback itself. In our analysis of 15,891 APP comments, leadership communication, transparency in decisions, and departmental communication emerged among the most frequently discussed topics. While APPs described a range of workforce challenges, many comments reflected a common frustration: Decisions that affected their work are made without sufficient APP input, visibility, or follow-through.

Those three items and comment findings are descriptors for a workforce that’s central to care delivery but peripheral to decision-making. Without visible leadership pathways and structured governance to participate through, APPs end up clinically essential but without a meaningful say in the things that impact them.

Organizations building enterprise APP leadership structures and standardized governance models are starting to close that gap. When APP roles are clearly defined and applied the same way, APPs practice at the top of their license, collaborate more effectively within multidisciplinary teams, and develop a stronger sense of professional belonging.

Clarifying the APP role pays off in several ways. Organizations that get it right expand patient access, impact patient experience, and improve APP retention and engagement.

6 things leading organizations do differently

The strongest performers have made an important shift in thinking: They’ve stopped treating APP strategy as a staffing question and started treating it as an enterprise governance and leadership question.

Rather than focusing solely on recruitment and coverage, they are building the leadership structures, operational support, and development pathways APPs need to thrive and contribute at the highest level.

These organizations are:

  1. Building enterprise APP governance and leadership structures: Establish dedicated APP leadership with executive sponsorship, clear operational accountability, and system-level oversight.
  2. Increasing leadership visibility and APP representation: Give APPs a meaningful voice in organizational decision-making through participation in executive forums, governance committees, and strategic initiatives.
  3. Strengthening two-way communication and engagement: Create formal, reliable channels for listening to APPs and communicating organizational priorities, decisions, and progress.
  4. Advancing data-driven workforce planning: Align staffing and deployment models with workload, patient acuity, access needs, and the full capabilities of the APP workforce, instead of relying on headcount alone.
  5. Optimizing practice models, workflows, and technology: Design roles, workflows, team structures, and technology around how APPs practice, removing barriers that limit efficiency, access, and top-of-license care.
  6. Creating clear career and professional growth pathways: Invest in APP-specific education, leadership development, recognition, and advancement opportunities that enable APPs to envision a long-term future within the organization.

These recommendations align closely with the AHA’s APP leadership structure principles , which provide additional detail around developing a more mature and integrated APP leadership model.

Ultimately, these priorities aren’t solely about improving the APP experience. They directly influence access, workforce stability, patient outcomes, and organizational performance.

APPs are increasingly central to healthcare’s ability to solve its most pressing workforce and access challenges. Organizations that create the conditions for APPs to do their best work will be better positioned to retain critical talent, expand access, improve outcomes, and sustain growth in the years ahead.

This work is significant—and we’d like to help. Our employee experience consultants work with organizations to find the root causes behind disengagement, segment workforce data down to the APP level, and build targeted action plans from what it shows. Speak to an expert, and we’ll work through your specific challenges together.
